BLUF: Gen Z Uprisings equal Useful Idiots strategy; domestic analysis. Everything, Everywhere, All At Once confidence up from 20% to 30% within next 12 months.

---
BEAR INDEPENDENT
BRIEF

Young people are toppling governments around the world at a scale we haven't seen before. Over the past year, youth-led protests have forced regime changes and sparked resignations in countries across multiple continents. What started in Kenya and Indonesia has spread to Nepal, Madagascar, Peru, Morocco, the Philippines, and most recently Bulgaria and Hungary, creating what is being called an unprecedented global movement of Gen Z political action.

An Atlantic Council report detailed the pattern. In Kenya, protests erupted over rising prices, youth unemployment, and corruption after new tax hikes were announced in 2024. Indonesian youth took to the streets over high parliamentary allowances and widespread food poisoning from government school meal programs. Philippine demonstrators mobilized in September over misallocated flood relief funds. In Nepal, young people "burned the parliament building and ousted the sitting government on September 9" after the government banned social media. Madagascar's youth protests over water and electricity failures "sent the president into exile and prompted a military-led government overhaul" just last month. Peru and Morocco are still seeing ongoing demonstrations—Peruvian youth protesting increased crime and corruption, while Morocco's "Gen Z 212" movement is angry about government funds being "directed toward preparations for the 2030 World Cup rather than public services."

As for the results, in Nepal and Madagascar, both countries experienced full regime change. However, in both cases, "the military stood by and allowed protests to oust the sitting government before ushering in transitional governments of their liking." The political influence of the young protesters "has diminished as new governing regimes have taken shape." Youth in Madagascar are frustrated that a career politician was chosen to lead the National Assembly, while Nepalese protest leaders say "they have been frozen out of the transitional government." In Kenya, protesters got President William Ruto to withdraw his tax bill but "failed to bring about the systemic change that many wanted."

The movement has now reached Europe. The Week reported how Bulgarian Prime Minister Rosen Zhelyazkov resigned on December 11 after mass protests against government corruption, making him "the latest in a slew of Bulgarian heads of government to step down in recent years." The demonstrations were sparked by a proposed tax increase but reflected "broader dissatisfaction with the government itself."

Hungary is facing similar unrest. Tens of thousands marched to Prime Minister Viktor Orban's offices demanding his resignation over alleged child abuse in state-run juvenile facilities. Videos emerged showing staff physically abusing children at a Budapest correction center, and prosecutors are investigating the former director for running a prostitution ring and subjecting minors to abuse.

What’s next? It seems other countries might see similar protests based on their demographics and political conditions. For example, Honduras and Côte d'Ivoire both have high youth populations, score above regional averages on political rights, but below average on prosperity indicators. As the Atlantic Council report noted, "Broadly, the data show that countries within the ‘low freedom’ and ‘low prosperity’ categories that have high youth populations and relatively well-protected political rights, and that perform relatively poorly in at least one indicator of prosperity, appear more prone to Gen Z demonstrations."

Of course, whether these uprisings can actually "make government more democratic, more accountable, and less corrupt in the long term" remains an open question. As the aftermath of the Arab Spring showed, "establishing more accountable democracies through youth mobilization will prove exceptionally challenging."
